nature-found-091.title: Produced, human and natural capital: three kinds of wealth
nature-found-091.text:
Roads and patents, skills and a sea view: {{ref:nature-hist-028}} sorts all of them into three kinds of capital. Economists confine the word to things that are measurable, and the range has widened over time. The general idea is covered in {{ref:nature-econ-083}}.

Roads, buildings, machines, ports and patents are tangible or intangible but alienable, meaning they can be sold on. Together they are called produced capital. Health, education and skills are intangible and cannot be handed to someone else. They form {{ref:nature-econ-531}}, which entered the list once ways were found to measure its value to individuals and society.

Natural capital, introduced earlier as {{ref:nature-found-010}}, became the third category once methods existed to measure the value people place on the materials and living systems of the earth. It runs from plants, which are tangible and alienable, to pollinators, a sea view and the global climate, which are intangible and not alienable.

The Review stresses a wedge between what sellers charge for these things, especially natural capital, and what they are really worth to society. That worth is the contribution an extra unit makes to the flow of social benefits, called the accounting value, or {{ref:nature-val-017}}. Many kinds of natural capital are unsold and free to the user, so special methods are needed to estimate it. Mainstream growth and development theories, and the models used by finance ministries and monetary authorities, leave out humanity's dependence on Nature.

nature-found-093.title: Why Nature does not maximise productivity
nature-found-093.text:
A portfolio manager would chase the highest yield. Nature does not. It maximises neither NPP, the net yearly growth of plant matter that feeds ecosystems, nor the regeneration rate of its ecosystems.

NPP per square metre differs by type of ecosystem: 0.75 kg a year in temperate grassy plains, 2.5 in {{ref:nature-eco-563}} and 0.14 in the ocean, because the abiotic environment varies. Even after allowing for that, planetary NPP is not at its maximum, and NPP in old growth forests is nearly zero. Life-form distributions emerged under selection pressures at the genetic level, not as an efficient spread of NPP. In the Review's fishery example, yield is zero at the long-run population K, so the marginal product of the fish stock there is negative.
